title: The Watchman and the Fall
sum: The chapter turns the book around. Ezekiel is made a watchman again (33:1-9), and the exiles, who say they are rotting in their guilt and ask how they can live, hear God swear that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and wants them to turn back and live (33:10-20). Then a survivor arrives from Jerusalem with the news that the city has been struck down, and Ezekiel's silence ends (33:21-22).

The last two oracles face the two groups the news creates. The people left in the ruins of Judah claim the land because Abraham was one man and they are many (33:23-29), and the exiles come to Ezekiel's house as to a concert, hearing his words and doing nothing (33:30-33). Everything before this chapter warned of the fall; everything after it is about what comes next.
readings: Read as history

The chapter is the book's hinge in time. The date in 33:21 sets the arrival of the news about five or six months after the city fell in the summer of 586 BC. The prophet's silence, promised in 24:27 to end when a fugitive came, ends as foretold, and from here the book speaks of rebuilding.
Read as a call to turn

The long middle (33:10-20) is a sermon with a simple point: the past does not decide the future. A righteous man who turns to evil loses his standing, and a wicked man who turns back lives. The exiles' despair, 'How can we live?', is answered as a question put to God and to them.

views.H: The twelfth year of Jehoiachin's exile (586-585 BC) is five or six months after the fall in the fourth and fifth months of 586 (2 Kings 25:3-9; Jeremiah 52:6-13). After the fall, Judah was a province of survivors under Gedaliah (2 Kings 25:22-26; Jeremiah 40-41); these are the 'people in the ruins' of 33:24.
views.C: Commentators describe the chapter as a joining of units: 33:1-9 repeats 3:16-21, 33:10-20 develops chapter 18, 33:21-22 is a short narrative that ends the muteness of 3:26-27 and 24:27, and 33:23-33 are two oracles on the people of the land and the exiles. Whether the pieces were joined by Ezekiel or an editor is debated.
views.J: Jewish tradition makes repentance (teshuvah) the way back to God, and the Talmud reads Ezekiel 18 and 33 among its texts on individual responsibility (Makkot 24a).
views.X: Christian readers hear 33:11 with 2 Peter 3:9 and 1 Timothy 2:4, and the watchman as the pastor who must warn (Acts 20:26-27; Hebrews 13:17). Churches differ on God's wish for everyone; see the card below.
views.F: For readers who expect a future restoration of Israel to the land, 33:21 is the turn from the past fall to the promises of chapters 34-48. Others read the whole of 34-48 as fulfilled in the return, the Second Temple or the church.

deep.h: Ezekiel's silence and the structure of the book
deep.b: Ezekiel was struck silent in 3:26-27, and 24:26-27 promised that on the day a fugitive came with the news of the fall, his mouth would open. That happens here (33:22). Between the two, he speaks only when the LORD tells him to: judgment against Judah in chapters 4-24 and against the nations in chapters 25-32. The three parts of the book (judgment on Jerusalem, oracles to the nations, restoration) are held together by this silence: when it ends, the tone changes from warning to promise. Whether Ezekiel could not speak at all, or could speak only God's words and not reason or plead with the people, is debated (see the note on 33:22).

Both chapters argue that each person is judged by his own way, and both quote the people's complaint that the LORD's way is 'not fair' (18:25, 29; 33:17, 20). Chapter 18 answers a proverb about fathers and children (see 18:2) and corrects the idea that the sins of one generation fall on the next. Chapter 33 is addressed to the generation that has already been judged: the question is not 'whose fault is this?' but 'how can we live?'. The Law says both things: God 'brings the fathers' guilt home to the children' (Exodus 20:5), and 'Each one is to be put to death for his own sin' (Deuteronomy 24:16). The Talmud (Makkot 24a) records that Ezekiel came and cancelled the saying of Moses in Exodus 20:5 with 'the life that sins will die' (18:4), and then asks how the two fit; Christian interpreters since the Fathers have also read them together, not against each other. See the topic on individual responsibility.

The base is the Leningrad Codex. For the Dead Sea Scrolls the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription (ETCBC dss) was read with tools/dss.py. In these seven chapters the only scroll with text is the Masada Ezekiel scroll (Mas 1d, before AD 74). Talmon's edition is reported to cover 35:11-38:14; the transcription has text for 35:11-36:35, 37:1-16, 37:23, 37:28 and 38:1-8, and a restored word is never counted as the scroll's reading. Chapters 33-34 and most of 38-39 have no scroll. Greek readings are from Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete, and a reading found only there is named by that codex. What is said of Papyrus 967 (it lacks 36:23c-38 and puts chapter 37 after 38-39) is as reported by Lust, Filson and Tov. The Syriac, the Targum and the later Greek translators are mentioned only as reported by named sources.

After the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC the Babylonians left a small population in Judah under a governor, Gedaliah, who was killed within months (2 Kings 25:22-26; Jeremiah 40-41). These are the people who say, 'There was one Abraham, and he came to own the land.' Their argument has force: God gave the land to Abraham, and they are the ones who stayed. Ezekiel does not deny the gift. He says the gift cannot be held by people who eat blood, bow to idols and shed blood, and that the land they hold will itself be turned into a waste. The answer in the next chapters (34-37) is that the land will be given again, to a purified people.

echoes: 3:16-21; 18:1-32; 24:25-27; 2 Kings 25:1-26; Jeremiah 52:4-16; Lamentations 1-5; Exodus 20:5; Deuteronomy 24:16; 2 Peter 3:9; Acts 20:26-27

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: Ezekiel, for the house of Israel in exile at Tel-abib
settings.when: The text gives no date; it stands in the twelfth year of the exile, just before the news of the fall (33:21), and some place it the evening before the survivor came (33:22)
settings.why: To remind Ezekiel that he alone is responsible for warning, not for the result: a watchman who sounds the horn has done his part, and the one who ignores it bears his own blood. It repeats 3:17-19.
settings.readers: Exiles reading the collected book saw that the prophet had warned them, and that the fall was not a surprise God hid from them.
views: A single speech to the prophet on the eve of the fall.
An editor placed a copy of 3:16-21 here to mark the second beginning of Ezekiel's ministry.

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: The house of Israel in exile, who have said they are wasting away in their guilt
settings.when: After the news of the fall, or just before it
settings.why: To answer despair with a way back: God takes no pleasure in anyone's death, and the past does not decide the future. It also answers the charge that God's way is 'not fair'.
settings.readers: Readers in every later exile, and the Jewish prayers of repentance, hear this as a promise that return is always open.

settings.to: The exiles at Tel-abib, who see the prophet speak again
settings.when: The fifth day of the tenth month of the twelfth year of the exile (about January 585 BC)
settings.why: To mark the end of the prophet's silence and the moment the book turns from judgment to restoration.
settings.readers: Readers of the book learned that the prophet had foretold the day (24:26-27).
views: Twelfth year (Masoretic Text, Greek); a few witnesses read the eleventh. See the variant.

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: Ezekiel, to be told to the exiles, about the survivors left in Judah
settings.when: After the fall, while Gedaliah's small province in Judah was struggling; the text gives no date
settings.why: To refute the claim that those who stayed own the land, and to show the exiles that the land is not secure with people who keep the sins that brought the exile.
settings.readers: Later readers saw both exiles and returnees warned that the land is held on conditions.

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: Ezekiel, about the exiles who come to hear him
settings.when: Undated; placed after the news of 33:21, as the exiles gather at his house
settings.why: To warn Ezekiel not to be misled by the crowds: they will hear and not do, until what he has said comes true.
settings.readers: Preachers and readers of every age have seen themselves in this audience; Jesus (Luke 6:46) and James (James 1:22-25) make the same charge.

traditions.q: Does God want every wicked person to repent and live?
views: God wants everyone to be saved, and 'God predestines no one to go to hell'; a person is lost only by freely turning away from God and persisting in it to the end (Catechism 1037).

God, the common Father of all, wills all to be saved; he chose for glory those he foresaw would use their free will rightly, and he condemns no one without cause (Confession of Dositheus, 1672, Decree 3).

God's call in the gospel is sincere and addressed to all, and he does not want anyone to perish; those who are lost are lost by their own unbelief and resistance, while election in Christ is a pure gift (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration XI).

The gospel call is serious and sincere, and God truly promises life to all who come (Canons of Dort III-IV, article 8); at the same time election is God's unconditional choice (Canons of Dort I, article 7), and Reformed teachers distinguish what God commands and invites from what he has decided.

Article 17 teaches that God chose some to life before the world began, and adds that his promises are to be received 'as they be generally set forth in Holy Scripture'. The article does not say how 33:11 and election fit together, and Anglicans have read the verse on both sides of that question.

Election is 'the gracious purpose of God' and is 'consistent with the free agency of man' (Baptist Faith and Message, 2000, article 5). The Confession does not say how 33:11 fits with it, and Baptists hold both Calvinist and non-Calvinist readings.
Grace is free for all and not only for some; God wills all to be saved, and people can resist him (Wesley, Free Grace).

title: The Shepherds and the One Shepherd
sum: The word 'shepherd' was a title for kings and rulers, and this chapter charges them with eating the flock they were meant to feed. They took the fat and the wool, left the weak and the lost, and ruled with force (34:1-10). So the LORD says, 'Here I am': he will search for his scattered sheep himself, gather them from the nations and feed them on the mountains of Israel (34:11-16).

The picture then turns to the flock itself, in which fat sheep push the weak aside, and God will judge between sheep and sheep (34:17-22). He promises one shepherd, 'my servant David', a covenant of peace, rain in its season and safety from wild animals and from the nations (34:23-31). The chapter is a base for Jesus' words about the good shepherd in John 10.
readings: Read as political critique

The shepherds are Judah's kings, officials and the priests and prophets who served them. The chapter explains the fall as the failure of leaders who used their position for themselves, and promises God as the true king.
Read as a messianic promise

The 'one shepherd, my servant David' (34:23-24) has been read in Judaism as the Messiah of David's line and in Christianity as Jesus, the good shepherd. Critical scholars often read it as a promise that David's house will rule again.

views.H: The shepherds include the last kings of Judah: Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah (2 Kings 23:36-25:7). The chapter was given after the news of the fall (33:21), when the survivors and the exiles asked who was to blame.
views.C: Commentators note the close link between Jeremiah 23:1-8 and this chapter, and some see a layered text in which 34:11-16 (God as shepherd) and 34:23-24 (the Davidic shepherd) were joined. The Greek and the Hebrew differ in details (34:3, 16, 29).
views.J: Jewish tradition reads 'my servant David' as the Messiah son of David and uses the shepherd as an image of God (Psalm 23:1). The Talmud debates whether the Messiah is a new David or David himself (Sanhedrin 98b).
views.X: Christian readers hear John 10:11-16 ('I am the good shepherd... one flock, one shepherd') and 1 Peter 5:2-4; elders and pastors are warned to avoid the shepherds' failings. The Roman Catholic lectionary reads 34:11-12, 15-17 on Christ the King, Year A.
views.F: Readers who look for a future restoration of Israel read 34:13-14 as the gathering to the land and 34:23-25 as the reign of the Messiah in the millennium; others read the same lines as fulfilled in the return and in Christ.

deep.b: The chapter's logic is a reversal. The shepherds 'shepherded themselves' (34:2, 8), so the LORD takes the work from them (34:10) and does it himself (34:11-16). Then he appoints one shepherd (34:23). Psalm 23, Isaiah 40:11 and Jeremiah 31:10 describe God as shepherd. Jesus claims both roles in John 10: he is the 'good shepherd' and he contrasts himself with the hired hand who runs when the wolf comes (John 10:11-13), a close echo of the shepherds who left the flock to wild animals (34:5, 8). The Christian pastor is both a sheep and a shepherd; 1 Peter 5:2-4 says that elders are to shepherd 'the flock of God' as examples and not for gain.

deep.h: David, the nasi and the king
deep.b: In 34:23-24 the future ruler is a 'shepherd' and then a 'leader' (nasi); in 37:22, 24 he is 'king'. The Plain says 'leader' for nasi (see the note at 34:24). The two titles may be deliberate: the ruler is a shepherd under God's own shepherding. The covenant of peace (34:25) is made with the flock. The Davidic promise of 2 Samuel 7:16 stands behind it, together with the promise of Jeremiah 23:5-6 and 33:14-17. See the topic on the Davidic covenant.

echoes: Jeremiah 23:1-8; Psalm 23; Psalm 80:1; Isaiah 40:11; Zechariah 10:2-3; Zechariah 11:4-17; Micah 5:2-5; Matthew 9:36; Luke 15:3-7; John 10:1-18; 1 Peter 5:2-4; Hebrews 13:20; Leviticus 26:1-13

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: Ezekiel, to speak against the rulers and leaders of Judah (the 'shepherds'), heard by the exiles
settings.when: After the fall of Jerusalem, when survivors asked who was to blame
settings.why: To name the failure of leaders as the reason the people were scattered, and to put the shepherds on notice that the LORD will take the flock back from them.
settings.readers: The Second Temple generation, and every community with leaders, could read this as a standing standard for those who hold power.
views: The kings (Jehoiakim, Zedekiah); the whole ruling class including priests and prophets (22:25-28); or any later leaders.

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: The scattered flock, the exiles, and within them the strong sheep who push others aside
settings.why: To promise that God will gather and care for the weak, and to warn that the flock too has fat and strong sheep who must be judged.
settings.readers: Readers in later exiles and in the church took the verses as a promise of God's own care.

settings.what: One shepherd, a covenant of peace
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: The house of Israel, in exile
settings.when: Same occasion, as the final part of the oracle
settings.why: To answer the loss of the Davidic king in 586 with a promise that David's house will lead again under God's care, and that the land will be safe and fruitful.
settings.readers: Later readers, Jewish and Christian, saw the Messiah here; see John 10.
views: A future king of David's line.
Jesus, the son of David and good shepherd.
A promise of renewed Davidic rule that may include more than one king over time.

title: Against Mount Seir
sum: A short oracle against Mount Seir, the hill country of Edom. Edom held an ancient hatred for Israel, poured out Israel's people to the sword in the hour of their final punishment, and said, 'The two nations and the two lands will be mine.' The LORD answers: 'But the LORD was there.' Edom will be a desolation, as Israel was.

The chapter works as the other half of chapter 36. Seir, which seized the land, is judged; the mountains of Israel, which were looted, are restored. It is also one of several oracles about Edom's role in the fall (25:12-14; Obadiah; Psalm 137:7).
readings: Read as history
Edom did take advantage of Judah's weakness (Obadiah; Lamentations 4:21-22), and the Nabateans later displaced it. The oracle explains why Edom's land would not be a refuge.
Read as a type
Edom stands for all who rejoice when God's people fall. This is how later Jewish and Christian readers used Edom, and why 36:5 speaks of 'all Edom' beside 'the rest of the nations'.

views.H: Edomites moved into the south of Judah after 586 BC. Nabatean Arabs took the Edomite heartland in the Persian period. The Edomites of Judah were later forced to become Jews by John Hyrcanus (about 125 BC), according to Josephus.
views.C: Commentators read 35:1-36:15 as one unit, with 36:1-15 as the counterpart of chapter 35. The Masada scroll preserves 35:11-15 and agrees with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling, but the Hebrew has a Ketiv/Qere at 35:9 ('will not be lived in' or 'will not return') (see the variants).
views.J: Jewish tradition read 'Edom' as Rome (a common rabbinic code), so this chapter was read as a promise against the empire that destroyed the second Temple. Edom as Esau's descendants is the older sense.
views.X: Christian writers took Edom as the enemies of the church and the world, and as Esau, who sold his birthright (Hebrews 12:16-17).
views.F: Isaiah 34 and Isaiah 63:1-6 make Edom a figure of God's final judgment on his enemies, and some readers apply that to the end of the age; others see the oracles as fulfilled in Edom's history.

echoes: 25:12-14; Genesis 25-27; Genesis 36; Numbers 20:14-21; Obadiah 1-21; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Malachi 1:2-5; Isaiah 34; Isaiah 63:1-6

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: Ezekiel, to speak against Edom, heard by the exiles
settings.when: After the fall of Jerusalem, and before the oracle to the mountains of Israel (36:1-15)
settings.why: To assure the exiles that nations which took advantage of their fall will pay for it, and that the land the nations claimed is still God's.
settings.readers: In the Second Temple period the oracle was read beside Obadiah and Malachi as a statement on Edom's fate.
views: The text has no date; it follows 33:21 and so is placed after the fall.

title: A New Heart and a New Spirit
sum: The chapter first speaks to the mountains of Israel: the enemy said 'Aha!', but they will bear fruit again, and people will fill them (36:1-15). Then God explains the exile. Israel made the land unclean, and when the exiles went to the nations they profaned his holy name, because people said, 'These are the LORD's people, yet they left his land' (36:16-21).

God will act, not for Israel's sake but for his holy name (36:22-23). He will gather them, sprinkle pure water on them, give them a new heart and a new spirit and put his own Spirit inside them, so that they walk in his rules (36:24-28). The land will be like the garden of Eden, and the people will be as many as a flock for sacrifice (36:29-38). The chapter is one of the most important in the Old Testament for the hope of a changed heart.
readings: Read as the end of exile

The promise answers the exiles' question in 33:10, 'How can we live?'. It is the restoration of Israel to its land, and also the inner change that would keep it there. God acts first, and the people are ashamed when they remember.
Read as new birth
John 3:5 (born of water and the Spirit), Titus 3:5-6 and Hebrews 10:22 hear baptism and the Spirit in 36:25-27. Churches differ on how the water and the Spirit are related; see the card below.

views.H: The oracle is set after the fall, to exiles still on the Chebar canal. The 'mountains of Israel' were being resettled by Judah's survivors and by neighbors (Edom among them, 36:5).
views.C: 36:23c-38 is absent from Papyrus 967 (early third century AD), which also puts chapter 37 after 38-39. The Hebrew words of 36:23-35 are in the Masada scroll, though much of 36:25-27 is restored there and does not count. Lust argued that 967 keeps the earlier form, with 36:23c-38 a later bridge written when chapter 37 was moved to follow chapter 36 (as reported by Hogeterp); Filson held that the Greek omission was deliberate. Many see 36:24-28 as the closest Ezekiel comes to Jeremiah 31:31-34.
views.J: The synagogue reads 36:16-38 (Sephardi: 36:16-36) on Shabbat Parah, the Sabbath before the month of Nisan when the red heifer chapter is read, linking the 'pure water' to the water of purification (Numbers 19).
views.X: Christian readers see the new heart and Spirit in the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 and Hebrews 8, and in baptism and the new birth. The Roman Catholic Easter Vigil reads 36:16-17a, 18-28.
views.F: Readers who expect a future return of Israel to the land take 36:24 and 36:33-36 as still to come; others read the promise as fulfilled in the return from Babylon and in the church.

deep.b: In 36:20-23 God says that he acts for his own name, which Israel profaned in exile. The nations saw Israel in exile and concluded that the LORD could not keep his own people in his own land. Moses used a similar argument to turn God from destroying Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 14:13-16). Here God uses the argument himself. The restoration will correct the nations' mistake by showing who he is. It is not about Israel's merit: 36:22 and 36:32 both say 'not for your sake'. Yet the result is for Israel's good: a land, a heart, a Spirit.

deep.h: The new heart, the new covenant
deep.b: Ezekiel 36:25-27 does not use the word 'covenant', but the verses sit beside the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31-34 and Deuteronomy 30:6 (God will circumcise the heart). 36:28 gives the covenant formula, 'You will be my people, and I will be your God'. The three texts together make the topic 'covenant' for readers who follow the thread. Ezekiel 18:31 told the people to 'make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit', and chapter 36 says God will give them. Both belong to the book, and readers have harmonized them as command and promise, as God's work and human turning. See the topics on covenant and the new birth.

deep.h: The Greek order and the long section
deep.b: Papyrus 967, the oldest Greek witness, is reported to lack 36:23c-38 and to place chapter 37 after chapters 38-39. Three explanations are given, each in its strongest form. Lust argued that 967 keeps the earlier form, with 36:23c-38 a later bridge written when chapter 37 was moved to follow chapter 36; the section would have no job in an order where 37 follows 39, and an accidental loss of so long a block is hard to believe. Filson argued that the translator or a reviser who had the full Hebrew left the section out on purpose. A third view is that the Greek translated a Hebrew source that did not yet have the section; whether that source was earlier or later is then the question. The Masada scroll has visible words of 36:23-35 in Hebrew before AD 74 (see the variants at 36:23 and 38:1), so the section is not a late addition to the Hebrew. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

deep.h: A word about the simile of 36:17
deep.b: The comparison to a woman's monthly uncleanness uses the language of priestly purity, in which the period caused ritual uncleanness, not shame or sin. Ezekiel was a priest, and his image says that Israel's conduct made the land unfit for the holy God, as a ritual impurity makes a person unfit for the sanctuary until cleansed. Readers have rightly noticed that the comparison can hurt, and commentators treat it with care.

echoes: Deuteronomy 30:1-6; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Jeremiah 32:37-41; Ezekiel 11:19-20; 18:31; 37:14; 39:29; Numbers 19; Psalm 51:7, 10; Isaiah 51:3; Joel 2:28-29; John 3:5; Titus 3:5-6; Hebrews 10:22; 2 Corinthians 3:3; Romans 8:4; Revelation 21:3; Romans 2:24

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: The mountains and valleys of Israel, as a way of speaking to the exiles
settings.when: After the fall; a counterpart to chapter 35 and to the oracle against the mountains in chapter 6
settings.why: To tell the exiles that the land the nations mocked and looted will bear fruit again and will be filled with people, so that they can plan to return.
settings.readers: Returned exiles in the Persian period could read this as a promise coming true as the land filled up again.

settings.what: For the sake of my holy name
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: The exiles ('the house of Israel'), who had said they were rotting in their guilt (33:10)
settings.when: After the fall; the book gives no date
settings.why: To explain that the exile was just, that God will restore his people for his own name, and that he will change their hearts so that they do not repeat the sin.
settings.readers: The passage became the haftarah for Shabbat Parah, and Christians read it in the Easter Vigil and at baptism; the Second Temple community saw it as the inner side of the return.
views: 36:23c-38 may be an expansion of an older, shorter text, as Lust argued from Papyrus 967; others hold that the Greek left it out. The Hebrew and the later Greek have it.

traditions.q: Does Ezekiel 36:25-27 describe baptism and the new birth?
views: Yes: baptism is the sacrament of rebirth by water and the Spirit and washes away sin, and Titus 3:5 'the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit' is quoted for it (Catechism 1213-1215); the Church reads Ezekiel 36:16-28 at the Easter Vigil, when the catechumens are baptized.
Yes: baptism is the sacrament in which a believer dies to the life of sin and is born again of the Holy Spirit to a holy life (Philaret's Longer Catechism).

Yes: baptism gives forgiveness of sins, rescues from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe; it is a new birth, with Titus 3:5-8 as the key text (Luther, Small Catechism).
Baptism is a sign of 'regeneration or new birth', and those who receive it rightly are grafted into the Church (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 27).
Baptism is a sign and seal of washing and regeneration, but the Spirit's regenerating work is not tied to the moment of the water (Heidelberg Catechism 69-73; Westminster Confession 28.6).
The new birth is the inward change, and baptism is its outward sign; Wesley taught that the two are not the same thing (The New Birth, sermon 45).

No: regeneration is 'a work of God's grace' in which the Spirit changes the heart and the sinner answers in repentance and faith (Baptist Faith and Message, 2000, article 4). Baptism follows as an act of obedience that pictures what has already happened in the believer (article 7).

title: Dry Bones and Two Sticks
sum: The hand of the LORD carries Ezekiel by the Spirit to a valley full of very dry bones. 'Son of man, will these bones live?' 'Lord GOD, you are the one who knows.' He prophesies to the bones, and they come together with a rattling, sinews and flesh and skin cover them, and then he prophesies to the breath, which comes from the four winds, and they stand up, a vast army (37:1-10).

The bones are the whole house of Israel, who say, 'Our bones have dried up, our hope has vanished.' God will open their graves, bring them to their land and put his Spirit in them (37:11-14). A second sign follows: two pieces of wood, one for Judah and one for Joseph, joined into one in Ezekiel's hand, show that Israel and Judah will be one nation under one king, David, with a covenant of peace and a sanctuary among them forever (37:15-28).
readings: Read as national restoration

The chapter explains itself: the bones are Israel in exile, and the graves are the exile (37:11-12). The vision answers the exiles' despair. It does not need a doctrine of individual resurrection, though it prepares for one.
Read as resurrection

From the first century the vision was heard as a promise of the resurrection of the dead. The Talmud debates whether the dead really rose (Sanhedrin 92b), church fathers cited it for bodily resurrection, and Jewish and Christian liturgies read it at Passover and at Easter.

views.H: The vision belongs after the fall of Jerusalem, when the exiles said that their hope was lost. The second sign answers the old split between Judah and Ephraim, and the 'king' who will reunite them is David's heir.
views.C: Critical scholars see a national metaphor, and debate whether the graves language already holds the idea of individual resurrection (Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2 come later). The Masada scroll has 37:1-16, 23 and 28 in the transcription; Papyrus 967's reported order puts chapter 37 after 38-39.
views.J: The Talmud records three views: the dead rose, sang and died; it was a parable; and they went to Israel and had children (Sanhedrin 92b). The synagogue reads 37:1-14 on the Sabbath of Passover, and the Targum is reported to read the chapter as the resurrection.
views.X: Christian writers from the Fathers cite the chapter for bodily resurrection; Revelation 11:11 echoes 37:5, 10. The Orthodox read 37:1-14 at Holy Saturday vespers, and the Roman Catholic Church reads 37:12-14 on the Fifth Sunday of Lent, Year A.
views.F: Readers who look for a future restoration of Israel read the chapter in connection with the modern return of Jews to the land (a view held by some dispensational teachers). Others reject that connection and say the vision was fulfilled in the return from Babylon and in Christ.

deep.h: Breath, wind and Spirit in one word
deep.b: The Hebrew ruach is wind, breath and spirit, and 37:1-14 uses all three. English cannot hold the pun, and the Plain keeps 'breath' in 37:5-10, 'winds' for the four directions and 'Spirit' for God's own. The thread leads from 36:26-27 ('a new spirit... my own Spirit') to 37:14 ('my Spirit') and 39:29 ('I have poured my Spirit out'). The Greek pneuma and John 3:8 show the same double sense.

Papyrus 967 reads 36, 38-39, 37, 40, and omits 36:23c-38, as reported. The Hebrew (the Masoretic Text, with the Masada scroll's reported extent through chapters 36-38) and Codex Vaticanus read 36, 37, 38-39, 40. Lust argued that 967 keeps the earlier form, with 36:23c-38 a later bridge written when chapter 37 was moved to follow chapter 36; on that view the Masoretic order is the later one and puts the resurrection after the new heart. Either way the Plain keeps the Hebrew order, in which the bones answer the exile, and Gog is the last threat before the Temple vision. See the variants at 36:23 and 38:1.

Ezekiel's vision comes before the clearest Old Testament texts of individual resurrection: Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2. Hosea 6:1-3 speaks of revival 'after two days' as a figure for national restoration. Jon Levenson has argued that restoration of Israel and raising of the dead are closely linked in the Bible and in later Judaism, so that the national and the personal readings are not rivals. The book of Revelation (11:11) and Matthew (27:52-53) take the picture further; see the topic on resurrection.

Judah and Joseph (Ephraim) stand for the southern and northern kingdoms, split since Solomon's son Rehoboam. Ezekiel takes two pieces of wood and joins them in his hand. The LORD says he will take the northern tribes from the nations, join them to Judah and make one nation under one king. Latter-day Saints read the two pieces as the Bible and the Book of Mormon; the text says the sign is about people and about David (37:21-25). See the note at 37:19.

echoes: Isaiah 26:19; Hosea 6:1-3; Daniel 12:2; Psalm 104:29-30; Genesis 2:7; Job 10:11; Lamentations 3:18; Jeremiah 3:18; Jeremiah 31:6-9; Jeremiah 33:14-22; Isaiah 11:13; 2 Samuel 7; Matthew 27:52-53; John 3:8; John 10:16; Revelation 11:11; John 5:25-29; 1 Corinthians 15:51-52

settings.by: Ezekiel, in first-person narrative; the LORD speaks to him
settings.to: Ezekiel, for the exiles who said, 'Our bones have dried up, our hope has vanished' (37:11)
settings.when: After the fall of Jerusalem; the text does not date it, and it follows the news of 33:21
settings.why: To answer despair with a picture: a people that seems dead can be raised by God's word and breath.
settings.readers: Returned exiles, the synagogue and the church read it as a promise of restoration and of the resurrection of the dead.
views: The bones are Israel; the graves are the exile.
A promise of the raising of the dead, which the national image presupposes.
The vision uses resurrection as the pattern of national renewal.

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: Ezekiel, to act out before his people, who ask him what it means (37:18)
settings.when: After the fall; a sign-act in public
settings.why: To show the exiles that the old rivalry between Judah and Ephraim will end under one king, and that God's sanctuary will be among them forever.
settings.readers: Later readers saw the reunion of the tribes, the Messiah, or, for Latter-day Saints, two books of scripture.

title: Gog of Magog
sum: The LORD tells Ezekiel to face Gog, of the land of Magog, the chief leader of Meshech and Tubal, and to prophesy against him. God will turn him around, set hooks in his jaws and bring him out with a huge army: horses and riders, Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer, Beth-togarmah and many peoples (38:1-9). In the last years Gog will come against a land restored from the sword, a land of open villages and quiet people, to plunder (38:10-13).

But it is the LORD who brings him, so that the nations will know him when he shows his holiness through Gog (38:16). The earthquake, the swords turned on one another, plague, flood, hail, fire and sulfur end the invasion (38:18-23). Gog is the last threat to a restored Israel before the new Temple.
readings: Read as a future battle

Many Jewish and Christian readers see a coming war in which a northern power, with allies from the ends of the earth, attacks Israel and is destroyed by God. They differ on when: after the return, in the days of the Messiah, or at the end of history.
Read as a symbol

Others read Gog as a figure for all the forces opposed to God's people, not a nation: Augustine read Gog and Magog as the nations of the whole earth (City of God 20.11). The names are drawn from real peoples, but the picture, a gathering from all four corners, is a type.

views.H: The names are Anatolian and other peoples known to Ezekiel's world (Genesis 10; Ezekiel 27); Gog may echo Gyges of Lydia, whom the Assyrians called Gugu, but none of the identifications is certain. The oracle is undated, and it sits between the restoration of chapters 34-37 and the Temple of 40-48 (dated 573 BC).
views.C: Zimmerli and others hold that 38-39 grew in layers, with a later 'proto-apocalyptic' element; Block, Greenberg and others hold that it is Ezekiel's own, a final statement about the nations. The Greek and the Hebrew agree on most of the chapter, and the Masada scroll has text of 38:1-8 in the transcription.
views.J: The sages speak of the war of Gog and Magog (Berakhot 7b) as part of the days of the Messiah, and the synagogue reads 38:18-39:16 on the Sabbath of Sukkot.
views.X: Revelation 19-20 draws on this chapter but changes it (see the note at 39:6). Christian readers have identified Gog with the Goths (Ambrose), the Turks (many Reformation writers) and Russia (nineteenth and twentieth century), or with all the world's enemies of the church (Augustine).
views.F: Dispensational teachers see a future invasion of restored Israel and often name Russia; others expect a final world war at the end of the age; others see Revelation 20 as the only battle. The Plain does not argue for any of these.

deep.b: Revelation 20:7-9 says that when the thousand years are over, Satan will deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, 'Gog and Magog', to gather them for the battle, and fire comes down from heaven. Ezekiel's Gog is a person of a particular land; Revelation's Gog and Magog are nations. Ezekiel's battle is on the mountains of Israel and followed by months of burying; Revelation's is around 'the camp of the saints and the beloved city'. John reuses Ezekiel's picture for a different scene. Whether the two scenes are the same event, the same event in different words, or different events is where Christian traditions differ (see the card on this chapter).

The two chapters belong to the genre often called apocalyptic or proto-apocalyptic: a final battle, a gathering from the ends of the earth, cosmic signs, a divine victory without any human army. The old prophets speak of an enemy from the north (Jeremiah 6:22), and Ezekiel gives this enemy a name. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, 'chief leader of Meshech and Tubal' (see the variant), and avoids identifying Gog with any one nation.

The nations in Gog's army and among the watching merchants are the same ones that appear in Genesis 10 (the table of nations) and in Ezekiel 27 (Tyre's trade). Meshech and Tubal and Gomer and Beth-togarmah are in Anatolia and beyond; Persia is east; Cush and Put are south, in Africa; Sheba and Dedan are in Arabia; Tarshish is the far west. Together they surround Israel on every side. The oracle then says that all of them, however far, come to the same fate. See the topic on the table of nations.

echoes: Genesis 10:2-5; Jeremiah 4:5-6:26; Joel 2:1-11; Joel 3:1-16; Zechariah 12:1-9; Zechariah 14:1-5; Isaiah 24-27; Psalm 2; Revelation 16:12-16; Revelation 19:17-21; Revelation 20:7-10

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: Ezekiel, to prophesy against Gog; heard by the exiles
settings.when: The book gives no date; it stands after the restoration (34-37) and before the Temple vision of 573 BC
settings.why: To assure the exiles that after the return, Israel's peace will not be broken for good: a last enemy will come, and God himself will destroy it for the sake of his name.
settings.readers: On the critical view that the chapters took shape in the Persian period, readers in a small, unwalled Judea could take comfort from the picture of God's defense; later readers made Gog a figure of the end.
views: Ezekiel foretold a future invasion and defeat.
The chapters were written or expanded in the Persian period as a picture of God's final defense of his people.
Gog is a type of every power that attacks God's people.

traditions.q: Who are Gog and Magog, and is Ezekiel's battle the same as Revelation 20's?
views: The Church has not defined who Gog is. Augustine, whom the Church has long followed on this point, read Gog and Magog as the nations of the whole earth against the Church (City of God 20.11). The Catechism speaks of a last trial of the Church and rejects an earthly millennial kingdom (Catechism 675-677) without naming Gog.

No Orthodox council has ruled on who Gog is. Andrew of Caesarea, whose Commentary on the Apocalypse became the standard Greek one, reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as the time of the church and Gog and Magog as the nations that rise against it at the end, not as one people on a map. The Book of Revelation is not read in the Orthodox public services.

Article 17 of the Augsburg Confession rejects the 'Jewish opinions' that the godly will take over the kingdom of the world before the resurrection, which rules out a thousand-year earthly reign. On Ezekiel itself, Luther's 1530 preface to chapters 38-39 read Gog as the Turk, the great enemy of Christendom in his day. The confession does not say who Gog is.

The Westminster Confession says nothing about Gog or the thousand years, so the answers come from teachers. Augustine's reading, followed by amillennial teachers such as Anthony Hoekema, makes Ezekiel's battle a picture of the same hostility and defeat that Revelation 20 shows. Postmillennial teachers, who expect a long age of the gospel's success first, take the last revolt of Revelation 20 as the final defeat of the world's opposition, and they differ on whether Ezekiel 38-39 was already fulfilled or points to it.

No Baptist confession fixes a view of Gog or of the thousand years. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 10) says Christ will return personally and judge, and does not name Gog; Baptists hold premillennial, amillennial and other readings.

Revelation 20 describes a final assault after the thousand years: the wicked are raised and, with Satan and his angels, surround the holy city, and fire from God consumes them (Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Belief 27). The statement does not mention Gog or Ezekiel 38-39.
Gog of Magog is a coalition of nations that will attack God's people; it is not Satan, in Ezekiel or in Revelation (The Watchtower, May 2015).

Historic (non-dispensational) premillennialists hold that Christ returns before a thousand-year reign on earth, and Revelation 20:7-10 is the last revolt of the nations at its end. George Eldon Ladd reads John as taking the names Gog and Magog from Ezekiel for that final assault, not for a Russian-led war earlier in the story.

Ezekiel 38-39 is a future attack on a restored Israel by a northern coalition, which they distinguish from the revolt after the thousand years in Revelation 20:7-9; the Scofield Reference Bible and Hal Lindsey identify the northern power with Russia, a reading that depends on taking 'Rosh' as a name.

title: The Fall of Gog
sum: The LORD says again that he is against Gog. He will turn him around, bring him up from the far north, knock the bow from his left hand and the arrows from his right, and Gog and his army will fall on the mountains of Israel. Fire will fall on Magog and on those living safely on the islands, and God's holy name will be known and not profaned again (39:1-8).

The weapons will be burned for seven years, and Israel will bury the dead for seven months in the Valley of Hamon-gog to make the land clean (39:9-16). The birds and wild animals are invited to a feast on the mountains of Israel, a sacrifice of warriors and the leaders of the earth (39:17-20). The nations will see that Israel went into exile for its guilt, God will turn Jacob's fortunes around, and he will not hide his face again, because he has poured out his Spirit (39:21-29).
readings: Read as the end of the nations' threat
The destruction is total and brings the nations to know the LORD. It closes the age of exile: the hiding of God's face (39:23-24) ends with the pouring of the Spirit (39:29).
Read as a vision of cleansing
The long burying and burning stress purity. The land must be cleansed before the Temple of 40-48 can be given, and Israel's work in these chapters is not fighting but burning and burying.

views.H: The chapter is a dramatic statement of what God would do for a restored people. The seven years and seven months are generally taken as large round numbers or symbols, and no known battle matches.
views.C: The chapter repeats parts of 38 (the turning, the northern origin, the fall on the mountains), which some take as a sign of two layers, and the closing summary (39:21-29) as a later conclusion tying the Gog story to the book's wider themes. Block holds that the chapter is Ezekiel's own.
views.J: The synagogue reads 38:18-39:16 on the Sabbath of Sukkot.
views.X: Revelation 19:17-21 takes the feast of the birds, and 20:7-10 the name Gog and Magog. Acts 2:17-18 quotes Joel's promise of the Spirit poured out, a promise 39:29 shares.
views.F: Readers who expect Gog's attack to be a future event place the seven years of burning in a future period and look for a political fulfillment; others read the chapters as a symbol of God's final victory over every enemy.

deep.h: Burning and burying: the work of Israel
deep.b: In chapters 38-39 Israel does not fight. God sends earthquake, plague, fire and the enemy's own swords. Israel's work is to burn the weapons (39:9-10) and to bury the dead for seven months, so that the land is clean (39:12-16). The burial valley will be named 'Hamon-gog', 'the horde of Gog', and a city nearby 'Hamonah'. The last act is a clean land. This links the chapter to the laws of corpse uncleanness (Numbers 19:11-16) and to the Temple of 40-48.

The last section reads like an end for the whole section 33-39, or even the whole book. It explains the exile for the nations (39:23-24), promises restoration (39:25-28) and ends with the Spirit poured out (39:29). The hiding of God's face has marked the exile since Deuteronomy 31:17-18. When the face is no longer hidden, the glory can return, and 43:1-5 shows it coming back to the Temple.

echoes: Numbers 19:11-16; Isaiah 34:6; Isaiah 54:8; Jeremiah 46:10; Joel 2:28-29; Joel 3:9-13; Zephaniah 1:7; Zechariah 12:10; Acts 2:17-18; Revelation 19:17-21; Revelation 20:7-10; Deuteronomy 31:17-18

settings.what: The fall of Gog and the burying
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: Ezekiel, to prophesy against Gog; heard by the exiles
settings.when: As in chapter 38, undated and set in the future from Ezekiel's time
settings.why: To describe how completely God will destroy the last enemy, and to promise that Israel will bury the dead and cleanse the land.
settings.readers: On the critical view that the chapters took shape in the Persian period, a small and weak community could read this as a promise of God's protection; later readers saw a final battle.

settings.what: The feast for the birds and animals
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: Ezekiel, to call the birds and wild animals
settings.why: To picture the enemy's destruction as God's sacrifice, in which warriors and rulers take the place of the animals.
settings.readers: Revelation 19:17-21 takes the scene as the great supper of God.

settings.what: Israel's exile explained, and the end of the hiding
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel the priest-prophet
settings.to: The house of Israel in exile, and the nations who watch
settings.when: As the end of the oracle against Gog and the whole section 33-39
settings.why: To tell the exiles that the exile was just, that God will restore them and that he will not hide his face again because his Spirit is with them.
settings.readers: Readers of the book at the return and in later ages found a summary of God's plan: exile, return, Spirit.
